section.title: Ehud and Shamgar
section.sectionRationale: The clean pattern of Othniel now turns again, and this time the narrator tells it with vivid, earthy detail and biting satire. Israel does evil once more, is handed to Eglon king of Moab, and cries out; God raises up an unlikely deliverer, Ehud, a left-handed Benjamite, who kills the fat king with a hidden blade and then routs Moab. A single verse then adds Shamgar, who strikes down six hundred Philistines with a farm tool. Together they show God saving through surprising, weak, and unexpected instruments.
section.thesis: God delivers His people not through the obvious or the impressive but through the overlooked and the improbable, a left-handed man from the tribe of the right hand and a farmer with an oxgoad, so that the deliverance is unmistakably His and the proud oppressor is brought low.
section.frameNote: Four beats: the servitude under Eglon of Moab, verses 12 to 14; the raising up and daring plan of Ehud, verses 15 to 23; the rout of Moab and the land's rest, verses 24 to 30; and the brief note of Shamgar, verse 31.

verses.text: Once again the Israelites did evil in the sight of the LORD. So He gave Eglon king of Moab power over Israel, because they had done evil in the sight of the LORD.
After enlisting the Ammonites and Amalekites to join forces with him, Eglon attacked and defeated Israel, taking possession of the City of Palms.
The Israelites served Eglon king of Moab eighteen years.

units.label: Ehud raised up with a hidden sword

verses.text: And again they cried out to the LORD, and He raised up Ehud son of Gera, a {{itter|left-handed}} Benjamite, as their {{moshia|deliverer}}. So they sent him with tribute to Eglon king of Moab.
Now Ehud had made for himself a double-edged sword a cubit long. He strapped it to his right thigh under his cloak
and brought the tribute to Eglon king of Moab, who was an obese man.
After Ehud had finished presenting the tribute, he ushered out those who had carried it.
But upon reaching the idols near Gilgal, he himself turned back and said, “I have a secret message for you, O king.” “Silence,” said the king, and all his attendants left him.
Then Ehud approached him while he was sitting alone in the coolness of his upper room. “I have a word from God for you,” Ehud said, and the king rose from his seat.
And Ehud reached with his left hand, pulled the sword from his right thigh, and plunged it into Eglon’s belly.
Even the handle sank in after the blade, and Eglon’s fat closed in over it, so that Ehud did not withdraw the sword from his belly. And Eglon’s bowels emptied.
Then Ehud went out through the porch, closing and locking the doors of the upper room behind him.

units.label: The rout of Moab and the land's rest
units.note: the LORD has delivered your enemies

verses.text: After Ehud was gone, Eglon’s servants came in and found the doors of the upper room locked. “He must be relieving himself in the cool room,” they said.

So they waited until they became worried and saw that he had still not opened the doors of the upper room. Then they took the key and opened the doors, and there was their lord lying dead on the floor.
Ehud, however, had escaped while the servants waited. He passed by the idols and escaped to Seirah.
On arriving in Seirah, he blew the ram’s horn throughout the hill country of Ephraim. The Israelites came down with him from the hills, and he became their leader.

“Follow me,” he told them, “for the LORD has delivered your enemies the Moabites into your {{yad|hand}}.” So they followed him down and seized the fords of the Jordan leading to Moab, and they did not allow anyone to cross over.
At that time they struck down about ten thousand Moabites, all robust and valiant men. Not one of them escaped.
So Moab was subdued under the hand of Israel that day, and the land had rest for eighty years.
After Ehud came Shamgar son of Anath. And he too {{yasha|saved}} Israel, striking down six hundred Philistines with an oxgoad.

itter.gloss: The phrase for Ehud's left-handedness means literally bound or restricted in his right hand. The irony is sharp: Ehud is a Benjamite, and Benjamin means son of the right hand, yet this son of the right hand is a left-handed man. What looks like a limitation is exactly what God uses, for a blade strapped to the right thigh would never be searched for on a left-handed man.

moshia.gloss: A deliverer or saviour, from the verb to save, yasha. As with Othniel, it is the LORD who raises up the moshia; the human deliverer, however unlikely, is God's chosen instrument. The same word describes the LORD Himself as Saviour, Isaiah 43:11, and points forward to the ultimate Deliverer, Jesus.

yad.gloss: Hand, power, agency. The word threads through the chapter: Israel is given into the hand of Eglon, and then the LORD delivers the enemy into Israel's hand, and Moab is subdued under the hand of Israel. The reversal of the hand marks who holds the power, and the passage makes plain that the deciding hand is the LORD's.

yasha.gloss: To save, deliver, rescue. The signature verb of the book: even Shamgar, given only one verse and armed with a mere farm tool, saved Israel. The word insists that rescue comes from God through whatever instrument He chooses, and it is the root behind the name Jesus, the LORD saves, Matthew 1:21.

basic.context: The cycle turns a second time. Israel does evil again, so the LORD strengthens Eglon king of Moab, who with Ammonite and Amalekite allies seizes the City of Palms, Jericho, and rules Israel eighteen years. When Israel cries out, God raises up Ehud, a left-handed man from Benjamin, the tribe whose name means son of the right hand. Ehud forges a short double-edged sword, straps it to his right thigh where no one would search a left-handed man, and gains a private audience with the enormously fat king under the pretense of a secret message. He drives the blade in, escapes, rallies Israel, and they cut down Moab at the Jordan fords, winning eighty years of rest. A single closing verse adds Shamgar, who strikes down six hundred Philistines with an oxgoad, a simple farm tool. The question the passage presses is: through whom does God save? And the answer is startling, through the unlikely, the overlooked, and the weak.
basic.hermeneutics: This is vivid historical narrative laced with satire against Moab and its bloated king. It must be read as description, not prescription: the text reports Ehud's assassination of a foreign oppressor as an act of God-sent deliverance in a specific redemptive-historical moment; it does not hand believers a mandate for political violence today. The narrator's earthy, even comic detail, the hidden blade, the fat swallowing the handle, the servants assuming the king is merely relieving himself, mocks the proud oppressor and magnifies the God who topples him through the least likely means.
basic.originalLanguages: Ehud is itter yad-yemino, literally bound in his right hand, that is left-handed, and the irony bites because he is a Benjamite, a son of the right hand. The LORD raises him up as a moshia, a deliverer. The word yad, hand, runs through the story: Israel is in Eglon's hand until the LORD gives the enemy into Israel's hand. And Shamgar, in a single verse, yasha, saved, Israel, the same root that stands behind the name Jesus.
basic.typology: These unlikely deliverers foreshadow the way God saves in Christ. God chooses the weak and the overlooked to shame the strong, and supremely He saves through a crucified Messiah, which looked to the world like weakness and folly. Ehud striking the enemy a decisive, hidden blow and Shamgar's improbable victory both anticipate the greater, stranger victory of the cross.
basic.christ: God delivers His people through an unexpected saviour who strikes the oppressor a mortal blow, then through a lone man with a farm implement. This pattern reaches its climax in Jesus, who saves not with obvious power but through apparent weakness, a carpenter's son, a crucified King, striking the true enemy a death blow at the cross, where God chose the foolish and weak things of the world to shame the strong and to save.
basic.god: God is just: He hands His idolatrous people over to Moab. He is merciful: He hears their cry and raises up a rescuer. And He is gloriously free in His choice of instruments: a left-handed assassin and a farmer with an oxgoad. By saving through such means He makes it unmistakable that the deliverance is His own, so that no one can boast in human strength.
basic.crossReferences: Numbers 22 to 24 recall Moab's earlier hostility to Israel through Balak and Balaam. Judges 20 notes the left-handed slingers of Benjamin, a tribal trait God turns to account. First Corinthians 1 explains God's pattern of saving through the weak and foolish things to shame the strong. And Matthew 1 names Jesus for the salvation, yasha, that all these deliverers foreshadow.
basic.oneStory: Israel sins again and is enslaved again, and again God raises up an improbable saviour to win them rest. The satire on mighty Moab and its fat king, undone by a hidden blade, and the farmer who routs the Philistines with an oxgoad, all proclaim that salvation is God's doing through instruments the world would never pick. It is one more turn toward the great deliverance, when God would save the world through a crucified Messiah, the ultimate unexpected Deliverer.

context.literary:
The second cycle is built on delay and withheld information, a technique the first cycle, Othniel's, barely uses. Verses 12 to 14 compress eighteen years of servitude into three sentences, the same brisk formula that closed the Othniel account in 3:7-11, evil, hand, years, rest. But once Ehud is introduced the pace slows to almost real time: the long walk with the tribute, the dismissal of the porters, the private word, the closed door, and finally the single stabbing sentence buried in the middle of all that description. The narrator then reverses the withholding: readers already know Eglon is dead, but the servants do not, and the story lingers over their assumption that the king is only relieving himself, their growing worry, and the search for a key. That gap between what the reader knows and what the characters know is the engine of the comedy and the satire.

The chapter also plays on wordplay the translation cannot fully carry. Ehud's tribe, Benjamin, means son of the right hand, yet he is bound in his right hand, and it is his left hand that saves Israel. The narrator names the idols near Gilgal as the turning point of Ehud's return, a small detail that recalls the stones of remembrance at Gilgal from Joshua's day and quietly contrasts true worship with the false gods of Moab. Shamgar's verse, by contrast, is narrative economy pushed to its limit, one line where Ehud's account fills nineteen. The two accounts, one expanded almost to slapstick, one compressed to a single line, make the same argument from opposite directions: the length of the telling has nothing to do with the size of the deliverance, since both flow entirely from the LORD who raises up whomever He chooses.
context.historical:
Moab lay east of the Dead Sea and had a long history of hostility to Israel. The City of Palms is Jericho, a strategic foothold west of the Jordan. Tribute, the payment Ehud brings, was the tax a subject people paid an overlord, and it gave him lawful access to the king. The oxgoad Shamgar wields was a long pointed stick used to drive oxen, an ordinary farm tool rather than a weapon, underscoring how God saves through the unimpressive.

Moab's presence west of the Jordan, occupying Jericho itself, the city Israel had destroyed under Joshua, was a humiliating reversal; ground Israel had once been given outright had fallen back into the hands of the very kind of nation Israel was meant to have driven out. The coalition Eglon assembles, Ammon and Amalek alongside Moab, verse 13, points to a broader alliance of Transjordanian and desert peoples pressing Israel from the east, the same peoples who reappear together against Gideon a few chapters later. Their route to Jericho along the fords near the Jordan explains why Ehud's men seize exactly those fords in verse 28, cutting off the escape of a defeated army back across the river to Moab.

The upper room where Eglon receives Ehud alone was likely a cooled roof chamber, a mark of luxury built to catch the breeze, matching the detail that the king was sitting in the coolness of his upper room, verse 20, and explaining why his servants assumed the locked door meant privacy rather than danger. Shamgar's oxgoad, a pointed staff long enough to drive a team of oxen and sometimes tipped with metal for clearing plow blades, was standard farm equipment, not a weapon of war, which is exactly the narrator's point in naming it rather than a sword.
context.canonical:
Ehud and Shamgar continue the downward cycle of Judges while displaying God's persistent mercy. The theme of God choosing the weak and unexpected instrument runs from these judges through Gideon's tiny band and David's sling to its climax in the crucified Christ, 1 Corinthians 1:27-29. The repeated giving into the hand and delivering out of the hand echoes the covenant blessings and curses and the Bible's larger story of bondage and rescue that finds its end in the greater exodus won by Jesus.

Moab's role as oppressor here is not an isolated note. Israel's uneasy history with Moab reaches back to Balak's hire of Balaam to curse the people, Numbers 22 to 24, forward through the following generations, and eventually to Ruth the Moabitess, who is gathered into the very line of David and of Christ, a striking reversal of this chapter's hostility. The eighteen years of oppression and eighty years of rest fit the pattern of covenant curse and blessing set out in Deuteronomy 28, where subjection to foreign nations is named as discipline for forsaking the LORD, and rest in the land as the fruit of returning to Him.

Shamgar's brief verse also anchors the Philistines as a recurring enemy long before Samson or Saul, showing that the threats named across the whole book, Moab, Ammon, Midian, Philistia, Canaan, were already gathering from every side of Israel's borders. The book of Ruth opens, deliberately, in the days when the judges ruled, and by naming Moab there the narrator invites the reader to hold Ehud's Moab and Ruth's Moab together, one age receiving judgment, the next receiving an unlikely daughter who becomes an ancestress of the Messiah.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
To show, with vivid and satirical narrative, that God saves His people through surprising and improbable instruments, humbling a proud oppressor and making plain that the deliverance is His, so that the reader marvels at the God who topples the mighty through the overlooked.

The narrator also means his hearers to feel the shame of Israel's history before they feel any pride in Ehud's cunning. A generation that had once destroyed Jericho under Joshua is now paying tribute inside its walls to a foreign king, and the storyteller wants that reversal to sting before the deliverance ever begins. By dwelling so long on Eglon's size, his soldiers' assumption about the smell in the cool room, and the fumbling search for a key, the account is shaped to make its first hearers laugh at the oppressor even as they are meant to tremble at how easily their own sin had handed them over to him in the first place. The point is not that cleverness saves, since cleverness belongs to Ehud, but that the LORD who raised up Othniel without any drama at all now raises up a devious, unlikely man and still gets exactly the same result, rest for the land, so that no reader can credit the method rather than the God behind it.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
What Ehud does to Eglon belongs to the era of holy war under the old covenant, when the LORD Himself commissioned particular acts of judgment against particular oppressors at particular moments; the account records that commissioning, verse 15, rather than laying down a timeless rule for how believers should treat rulers they dislike. Reading Ehud's cunning as a pattern for personal conduct would miss that the whole point of the narrator's comic detail is to magnify the LORD's freedom to topple pride however He chooses, not to supply a method for anyone else to copy.

This distinction matters because the chapter is not shy about the violence, or about celebrating it: verse 29 counts ten thousand Moabite dead without apology, and verse 31 credits Shamgar with six hundred more. Readers who turn this into a manual for personal or political violence miss that these are acts of holy war under a covenant arrangement that ended with the coming of Christ, who told Peter to put away the sword, Matthew 26:52, and who overcomes His enemies now by the proclamation of the gospel rather than the edge of a blade. What is meant to be copied is Israel's cry in verse 15 and the posture that follows it, a readiness to act the moment God's word comes, to follow a leader who calls in the LORD's name, and to trust that the outcome belongs to God rather than to the size of one's own sword or the cleverness of one's own plan.

debates.question: How should we read Ehud's deception and killing of Eglon, morally?

views.label: A God-sent deliverance to be received, not copied
views.case: The narrator frames Ehud as a deliverer whom the LORD raised up, and the killing as the means by which God freed His oppressed people in a specific covenantal moment of holy war; it is reported approvingly within that redemptive-historical setting, not offered as a timeless ethic of political murder.

views.label: A morally tangled act the text does not sanitize
views.case: Scripture records the cunning, the concealed blade, and the gruesome detail without moralizing, and honesty requires us to feel the tension; the passage shows God working through flawed and violent human means without endorsing every feature of them, much as it does elsewhere in Judges.

debates.bearing: Either way the deliverance is God's and the violence belongs to the world of holy war under the old covenant; Christians read it as description that magnifies God's saving power, not as license, and they long instead for the King who overcomes His enemies by dying for them.

debates.question: Why does the text dwell on Ehud's left-handedness and Eglon's obesity?

views.label: Deliberate irony and satire
views.case: The Benjamite, son of the right hand, is left-handed, and the fat king is undone by the very blade his guards would never find; the details are pointed irony that mocks proud Moab and delights in God's surprising method of rescue.

views.label: Realistic detail that explains the victory
views.case: The left hand explains why the sword on the right thigh escaped detection, and the king's size explains why the blade was swallowed whole; the details are not merely comic but the concrete means by which the plan succeeded under God's providence.

debates.bearing: Both readings serve the same point: what looked like Ehud's limitation was exactly what God used, teaching that God's deliverance often comes through what the world overlooks or despises.

study.originalLanguages:
The story is built on a few telling words. Ehud is described as itter yad-yemino, literally bound or restricted in his right hand, and the phrase drips with irony because Ehud belongs to Benjamin, a name that means son of the right hand; the son of the right hand is a left-handed man, and that very trait is what God uses, since no one would search for a blade on the right thigh of a left-handed man. The LORD raises him up as a moshia, a deliverer or saviour, the same word used of Othniel and of the LORD Himself. Running through the whole chapter is the word yad, hand, which means hand, power, and agency: Israel is given into the hand of Eglon, then the LORD gives the enemy into Israel's hand, and Moab is finally subdued under the hand of Israel. The shifting of the hand tells you who holds the power, and the answer is the LORD. Finally, of Shamgar, armed with nothing but an oxgoad, the text simply says he yasha, saved, Israel, the signature verb of the book and the root behind the name Jesus, the LORD saves.

A few other words sharpen the satire. The idols Ehud passes twice, at Gilgal in verse 19 and again in his escape in verse 26, are pesilim, carved images, from the verb pasal, to hew or carve; the word marks them as mere handmade objects even as it marks the spot as the hinge of the plot, the place where Ehud turns back to do God's business rather than Moab's. Twice Ehud tells the king he carries a dabar for him, a secret dabar in verse 19 and a dabar from God in verse 20; dabar can mean either a word or a thing, so that the sentence is true in both senses at once, Ehud brings a verdict from God, spoken, and he brings the sword, a thing, plunged into the king. Even Eglon's own name likely comes from egel, a young bull or calf, so that the fattened king carries, in his very name, the picture of an animal being led toward slaughter, and the narrative brings that picture home.

The chapter's insistence on yasha and moshia, save and deliverer, for both Ehud and Shamgar, despite their utterly different weapons and their utterly different amount of narrative attention, argues that the word of salvation belongs to the LORD rather than to any particular kind of hero, whether the elaborate deceiver or the anonymous farmer with his tool still in hand.

typology.type: The unlikely, overlooked deliverer who strikes the oppressor a decisive blow
typology.fulfillment: Christ appeared in weakness and lowliness, born in an occupied province to a family of no standing, and struck the true enemy, the devil who holds the power of death, a mortal blow not with a hidden blade but by dying Himself, Hebrews 2:14-15. As Ehud walked in alone where no one expected danger and left the door shut behind him, so the true blow against the ancient enemy fell where the world least expected victory to be won, on a Roman cross, and it fell decisively enough that the enemy could never rise again, Colossians 2:15.

typology.type: The single lowly instrument, an oxgoad, winning a great victory
typology.fulfillment: God saved the world through the folly and weakness of the cross rather than through any weapon of human power, so that no flesh may boast in His presence, 1 Corinthians 1:25-31. Just as an oxgoad meant for driving cattle became, in the LORD's hand, an instrument of national deliverance, so a Roman instrument of shame and execution became, in God's hand, the very means of the world's rescue, proof that the LORD needs no impressive tool to accomplish an impossible victory.

typology.type: The enemy given into the hand of God's people
typology.fulfillment: Christ has handed His people a victory over sin, death, and the devil that they could never have won on their own, disarming the powers and authorities and putting them to open shame, Colossians 2:15. Just as Moab's fords were seized and its army given into Israel's hand so that not one man escaped, Judges 3:29, so the final defeat of every hostile power is already secured in Christ, and believers are told that the God of peace will soon crush Satan under their feet, sharing in a triumph that was never their own to begin with, Romans 16:20.

study.christ:
The way God saves here, through a left-handed man the enemy underestimated and a farmer with a cattle prod, is the very pattern that reaches its climax in Jesus. God delights to choose the weak and the overlooked to shame the strong, and He did so supremely in a crucified Messiah, 1 Corinthians 1:27-29. Ehud struck the oppressor a hidden, decisive blow and then led his people out of bondage; Christ struck the true oppressor, the devil who held the power of death, a mortal blow at the cross, and leads His people out of a far deeper slavery, Hebrews 2:14-15. Shamgar's improbable victory with a mere oxgoad shows the same principle that the cross displays in full: God saves by means the world calls foolish, so that salvation is unmistakably His and no one can boast. Where these deliverers won a rest that later lapsed, Jesus, the true and final Deliverer, wins a rest that never ends.

Notice, too, what Ehud does not do. He does not raise an army before he acts; he goes alone, unarmed in the eyes of the watching guards, carrying nothing but tribute and a hidden blade strapped where no one thinks to look. Jesus likewise went to His decisive battle without visible weapons and without an army, entering Jerusalem on a donkey rather than a warhorse, and was struck down looking, to every observer, like a defeated man rather than a conqueror. Only afterward does the true nature of what happened become clear, just as only after Ehud has escaped to Seirah and sounded the horn does Israel understand that their oppressor is already dead and their deliverance already accomplished.

There is also a foretaste of resurrection joy in the shape of the story: word of Eglon's death precedes the full victory, and it is that news, carried by a rescued man's own voice, that gathers Israel to claim what God had already won, much as the news of the empty tomb gathers the church to live out a victory secured before any of them lifted a hand. And Shamgar's single verse, tucked almost as an afterthought between two larger accounts, still insists that he too saved Israel, a small reminder that the gospel of God's saving work does not depend on how much space or attention a deliverer receives, since the smallest mention of salvation in Scripture carries the same weight as the largest, all of it gathered up at last in the one Deliverer named for saving, Jesus.
study.god:
God fills this account as its true actor. He is just, giving His idolatrous people over to Eglon of Moab exactly as their sin deserved, and letting the servitude run eighteen long years. Yet He is merciful, hearing their cry and raising up a rescuer without delay. And He is sovereignly free in the instruments He chooses: not a mighty warrior of obvious strength but a left-handed man and, in a single verse, a farmer with an oxgoad. By stooping to save through such unlikely means, God makes the deliverance transparently His own work, mocking the pride of the strong and refusing to let human power take the credit. The reversal of the hand, from Eglon's grip to Israel's, shows that the deciding power was never Moab's and never merely Ehud's, but the LORD's, who gives the enemy into His people's hand.

This God is also patient with the passage of time itself. Eighteen years is a full generation's worth of servitude, long enough for children to be born who know nothing but tribute and oppression, and the narrative does not rush past that fact; it names the number plainly in verse 14 so that the reader feels the weight of the wait before feeling the relief of the rescue. When deliverance finally comes it comes all at once, an assassination completed in one line, an army broken in one battle, a rest that then lasts eighty years, more than four times the length of the servitude, a detail that quietly argues God's grace outlasts and outweighs His judgment.

God is also the God who works through ordinary courage rather than supernatural spectacle in this chapter; unlike some other deliverances in the book, there is no fire from a rock, no fleece, no angel visibly appearing, only a man who forges a blade, walks back through a door, and blows a horn in the hills. The absence of visible miracle does not mean the absence of God; it means that His providence works as surely through a planned deception and a blown horn as it works through any wonder, a lesson worth remembering for readers who expect God's hand only in the dramatic.

crossReferences.note: Moab's fear and hostility toward Israel go back to Balak's attempt to hire Balaam to curse them as they approached the promised land, a plot that failed only because the LORD turned every curse into blessing. Eglon's oppression two centuries later shows that old hostility finally succeeding by force of arms instead of sorcery.

Benjamin, Ehud's own tribe, was famous for seven hundred left-handed men who could sling a stone at a hair's breadth and not miss, a detail that shows Ehud's left hand was not a solitary oddity but a recognized skill within his tribe, one that God used for deliverance here and for civil war there.
God chose the weak and foolish things of the world to shame the strong, so that no one may boast, the pattern seen in Ehud and Shamgar and fulfilled at the cross.
Christ shared in flesh and blood so that through death He might destroy the one who held the power of death and free those in slavery, the greater deliverance these judges foreshadow.

The angel tells Joseph to name Mary's son Jesus, for He will save His people from their sins, using the same root, yasha, that describes Shamgar saving Israel with an oxgoad; the smallest deliverer in Judges and the greatest Deliverer in the Gospels share one saving name.

The covenant curses warn that failing to serve the LORD with joy and gladness would mean serving hostile nations instead, in hunger and want; Eglon's eighteen year tribute over Israel is exactly this warning coming to pass in real history.

This psalm lists Moab among the ancient nations that conspired against Israel, recalling the same old animosity that put Eglon on Israel's throne in Jericho, and it prays for God to deal with such enemies as He dealt with them of old.

Samuel later recounts this very episode in his farewell speech, naming the king of Moab among the oppressors the LORD sold Israel to for forgetting Him, using Ehud's story as proof, generations later, that Israel's whole history has been forgetting and being rescued.

The book of Ruth opens in the very days when judges ruled and finds Israelites fleeing famine into the land of the same nation Ehud once fought, and brings home a Moabite woman who becomes an ancestress of David and of Christ, turning old hostility into unexpected grace.

Paul says Christ disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame by the cross, the ultimate answer to every scene in Judges where God strips an oppressor of his power through an unlikely and hidden means.

study.oneStory:
This chapter sits deep inside redemption's long middle, after the fall has done its damage and long before the new creation dawns, in the era when God is teaching a covenant people, generation after generation, that they cannot save themselves and that every deliverer they receive is itself a gift and a signpost. The specific sin behind Eglon's eighteen years is named back in chapter 2 as covenant unfaithfulness, chasing the gods of the peoples God had commanded Israel to drive out; the fall's basic pattern, distrust of God's word leading to death and servitude, replays itself on a national scale every time Israel does evil again.

What this passage sets up is a widening argument that runs through the rest of Judges: each generation's rescue is more compromised, each deliverer more flawed than the last, so that the reader is prepared to feel the ache behind the book's closing refrain, in those days Israel had no king. Ehud's devious blade and Shamgar's crude oxgoad are earlier, cruder answers to the same problem that will surface again in Gideon's fear, Jephthah's rash vow, and Samson's ruin, a spiral that argues no merely human judge can be the final rescuer Israel needs.

And this passage reaches toward new creation precisely because it refuses to let human strength take credit. A left-handed man and a farmer with a cattle prod cannot be mistaken for self-made heroes, so every reader down the centuries is pushed past them toward the one Deliverer in whom weakness itself becomes the very shape of victory, and toward the last chapter of the story, where every enemy is finally and permanently subdued and rest never again lapses into eighty years or eighteen, but lasts forever.

quiz.q: Why did Israel come under the power of Eglon king of Moab?

options.text: Because the Israelites again did evil in the sight of the LORD.
options.note: Verse 12 states plainly that God gave Eglon power over Israel because they did evil.

options.text: Because Moab had formed a strong alliance with Ammon and Amalek.
options.note: Eglon did enlist those allies, verse 13, but the stated reason for the servitude is Israel's sin.

options.text: Because Israel had no weapons to defend itself.
options.note: The text does not blame a lack of weapons; it names Israel's evil as the cause.

options.text: Because the LORD was powerless against Moab's gods.
options.note: The LORD Himself gave Eglon the power and later took it away; He is sovereign throughout.

quiz.q: How did Ehud's left-handedness matter to the deliverance?

options.text: He hid the sword on his right thigh, where guards would not search a left-handed man, and struck by surprise.
options.note: Verses 16 and 21 show the concealed blade drawn with the left hand; the trait was key to the plan.

options.text: It made him a more skilled and dangerous fighter overall.
options.note: Benjamites were noted for left-handed skill, but the point here is the concealed, unsearched blade.

options.text: It was an incidental detail with no bearing on the story.
options.note: Far from incidental, it is the very feature God used to accomplish the rescue.

options.text: It meant he needed no weapon at all to defeat the king.
options.note: He forged and used a double-edged sword; the left hand is how he concealed and wielded it.

quiz.q: What does Shamgar's victory with an oxgoad chiefly teach?

options.text: God saves through unlikely, lowly instruments, so the deliverance is clearly His.
options.note: A farm tool striking down six hundred shows salvation comes from God, not impressive means.

options.text: That a determined person can overcome great odds.
options.note: There is boldness here, but the deeper point is that God saved through him, verse 31.

options.text: That farmers made the best soldiers in Israel.
options.note: This misses the theology; the oxgoad highlights God's power, not a class of soldier.

options.text: That skilled weaponry is the key to victory.
options.note: The opposite: an ordinary oxgoad, not fine weaponry, wins the day under God's hand.

quiz.q: How should we read the killing of Eglon by Ehud?

options.text: As a God-sent deliverance reported within the old covenant, described for us, not prescribed as a pattern to copy.
options.note: The narrator frames Ehud as a raised-up deliverer; it is description in a redemptive-historical setting, not a license.

options.text: As a rough act God used, which the text records honestly without sanitizing.
options.note: True to the earthy honesty of the text, but it understates that God Himself raised Ehud up to deliver.

options.text: As a timeless example that believers may take up violence for God's causes.
options.note: This wrongly turns description into prescription; the New Testament calls Christ's people to another way.

options.text: As proof that the Bible approves of murder in general.
options.note: The passage is a specific act of deliverance under holy war, not any blanket approval of murder.

quiz.q: How do Ehud and Shamgar point forward to Christ?

options.text: God saves through the weak and unexpected, foreshadowing salvation through the crucified Messiah who strikes the true enemy a mortal blow.
options.note: The pattern of God using the overlooked climaxes in the cross, 1 Corinthians 1:27-29 and Hebrews 2:14.

options.text: They show that God's deliverers are always mighty and impressive figures.
options.note: The reverse is true; their unlikeliness is the very link to Christ's saving through weakness.

options.text: They teach that deliverance is only political and military.
options.note: Their earthly rescue points beyond itself to Christ's rescue from sin, death, and the devil.

options.text: They have no bearing on Christ or the gospel.
options.note: The root yasha, to save, that describes Shamgar stands behind the very name of Jesus.

questions: God raised up a left-handed man from the tribe of the right hand, using the very thing others might have counted a weakness. Where might God be wanting to use what you consider your limitation for His purposes?
The narrative openly mocks proud, bloated Moab, undone in a moment. Where do you see the pride of the strong today, and how does it steady you to know that God topples it in His time?
Israel's rescue came only after they cried out to the LORD. What burden do you need to bring to God in an honest cry rather than trying to carry it alone?
Shamgar saved Israel with nothing more than a farm tool. What ordinary, unimpressive means has God placed in your hand that He might use for good if you offer it to Him?

These deliverers won a rest that eventually lapsed, but Christ saves through the weakness of the cross and wins a rest that never ends. How does the strange power of the cross reshape what you count as strength and weakness this week?

translationNotes.note: The City of Palms is Jericho, as the BSB footnote notes; it was a strategic stronghold west of the Jordan that Moab seized.
Left-handed renders a Hebrew idiom meaning restricted in his right hand; the irony is that Ehud is a Benjamite, and Benjamin means son of the right hand.
A cubit long is about eighteen inches or forty-six centimeters, per the BSB footnote; a short blade well suited to concealment under a cloak.
An oxgoad was a long pointed staff used to drive oxen, an ordinary farm implement, which underscores how God saved Israel through the humblest of means.
